answers.label: Q.1(a)
answers.finalAnswer: By doing our work with dedication, honesty and service; e.g. Anand Kumar's Super 30 made teaching seem second to none
answers.solution:
It is not the profession that makes us great; it is we who make our profession great. We do this by doing our work sincerely, honestly and for the good of others.

For example, Anand Kumar's Super 30 programme sent many underprivileged students to the IITs, and because of it the profession of teaching is seen as second to none. (Other examples from the passage: Captain Vikram Batra and Captain Manoj Kumar Pandey, who laid down their lives for the country, or the healthcare workers who risked their lives during the pandemic.)

answers.label: Q.1(b)
answers.finalAnswer: No; every profession is equally important, and only time and situation make one seem more important
answers.solution:
No, no profession can be considered the best. According to the passage, every profession is equally important, and it is only 'the nature of time and space' (the situation we are in) that makes one profession seem more important at a particular moment.

For instance, teachers are very important when we think of our children's education, doctors when we fall ill, and soldiers and the police when we think of the nation's security. So calling one profession 'head and shoulders above others' is preposterous.

answers.label: Q.1(c)
answers.finalAnswer: Have big dreams, work hard to achieve them, and become responsible and productive citizens
answers.solution: The passage advises young students to have big dreams and to pull out all the stops (make every possible effort) to achieve them. It also tells them that after achieving their dreams they must become responsible and productive citizens of their country; only then can they be considered assets of society.

answers.label: Q.1(d)
answers.finalAnswer: By being careless or misusing it; e.g. a doctor whose carelessness causes a patient's death
answers.solution:
We make our profession look bad when we are careless in our work or use it to harm others.

For example, if a patient dies in a hospital because of a doctor's carelessness, society will not feel great about the medical profession. Similarly, if a scientist develops a deadly virus to destroy mankind, people of his profession might be seen by the world as viruses.

answers.label: Q.1(e)
answers.finalAnswer: preposterous; assets; underprivileged
answers.solution:
(i) Ridiculous: preposterous ('...to consider a particular profession to be head and shoulders above others is definitely preposterous.')
(ii) Wealth: assets ('...they cannot be considered assets of the society.')
(iii) Deprived: underprivileged ('...sent many underprivileged students to IITs')

answers.label: Q.1(f)
answers.finalAnswer: head and shoulders above (others); pull out all the stops
answers.solution:
(i) To be a lot better than others: head and shoulders above (others) ('...to consider a particular profession to be head and shoulders above others...')
(ii) Make a lot of effort: pull out all the stops ('...they must pull out all the stops to achieve their dreams.')

answers.label: Q.2(a)
answers.finalAnswer: The Road I Have Taken
answers.solution:
A suitable title is 'The Road I Have Taken'.

The whole poem is about the road (path in life) the poet has chosen, the difficulties on it, and the decision to believe in it. (Other suitable titles: 'My Road', 'The Road of Life'.)

answers.label: Q.2(b)
answers.finalAnswer: The ride has been bumpy; the reality is harsher than he expected
answers.solution: The poet feels hesitant to go ahead because the journey on the road he has chosen has been bumpy (full of difficulties), and the reality of it has turned out to be a little harsher than he had imagined.

answers.label: Q.2(c)
answers.finalAnswer: They chose it thinking it was the road where he would travel fastest
answers.solution: The poet will not blame his family because they chose this road for him with good intentions. They thought it was the road on which he would travel fastest, that is, make the best progress in life.

answers.label: Q.2(d)
answers.finalAnswer: Because he used to love the road he chose
answers.solution: The poet will not blame himself because he chose the road out of love: 'No, I used to love it'. It was his own liking, even though the reality later proved a little harsher.

answers.label: Q.2(e)
answers.finalAnswer: Every path in life has difficulties; believe in your own path and stay hopeful
answers.solution: The poem tells us that no path in life is a bed of roses; even roads that look smoother and greener have their own puddles (problems). So we should not blame ourselves or others for the path we have taken. Instead, we should believe that our own road is the best and always look forward to the best with hope and confidence.

answers.label: Q.2(f)
answers.finalAnswer: Metaphor; rhetorical question
answers.solution:
1. Metaphor: the road stands for the path or career one chooses in life. 'Each road is a life' compares a road directly to life, and 'puddles' stand for problems.
2. Rhetorical question: the poet asks questions to make the reader think, not to get an answer, e.g. 'Should I go ahead or not?' and 'Should I blame myself for the road I have taken?'

(The poem also uses an idiom, 'not a bed of roses', meaning not easy or comfortable.)

answers.label: Q.2(g)
answers.finalAnswer: smoother; believe
answers.solution:
(i) Bumpy: smoother ('Though appear smoother and greener')
(ii) Disbelief: believe ('Believe that your road is the best')

answers.label: Q.3
answers.solution:
Manisha
C-24, Saket
South Delhi 110017

17 June 2023

The Editor
The Times of India
Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg
New Delhi 110002

Subject: How every resident can help make Delhi healthier

Sir/Madam,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to share how each resident of Delhi can help create a healthy environment in our city.

Delhi's air is among the most polluted in the world, and its garbage dumps keep growing. The government alone cannot solve these problems; every citizen must play a part. We can travel by Metro, bus or bicycle, or share cars, instead of driving alone. We must never burn leaves or garbage. Waste should be separated into wet and dry at home, and wet waste can be turned into compost. Each family can plant at least one tree and look after it. We should carry cloth bags instead of plastic ones, save water, and switch off lights and fans when they are not needed. Resident welfare associations can organise cleanliness drives in their colonies and parks.

If every one of us takes these small steps, Delhi can once again breathe freely.

Yours faithfully,
Manisha

answers.label: Q.4
answers.solution:
The Impact of ChatGPT on Education
by Arjun Rawat

ChatGPT, a computer program that can answer questions and write like a human, has entered our classrooms almost overnight. Its impact on education is both exciting and worrying.

On the positive side, ChatGPT is like a tutor that never gets tired. A student who does not understand a topic can ask it to explain again and again in simple words. It can suggest ideas for a project, correct grammar and translate difficult passages. Teachers can use it to prepare quizzes and lesson plans quickly, which leaves them more time for their students.

However, there are serious dangers. Some students copy whole essays and homework from it without learning anything. Its answers are sometimes wrong, yet they sound confident, so a careless student may believe false facts. Too much dependence on it can also weaken our own thinking and writing skills.

ChatGPT is a tool, like a calculator. Used wisely, to understand and to check our work, it can make learning richer. Used to avoid effort, it makes us poorer learners. Schools must teach students to use it honestly and sensibly.

answers.label: Q.5
answers.solution:
Topics chosen: (a) and (c).

(a) Child is the father of man

These words of William Wordsworth mean that the habits and qualities we develop as children shape the adults we become. A child who learns honesty, discipline and kindness at home and in school usually grows into a responsible citizen. On the other hand, bad habits picked up early are very hard to give up later. That is why childhood must be guided with great care. The seeds sown in a young mind decide the tree it grows into.

(c) A rotten apple spoils the barrel

This proverb means that one bad person can spoil a whole group. Just as one rotten apple makes the good apples around it rot, a single dishonest or lazy member can spread bad habits among others. In a class, one student who bullies or cheats can lead his friends astray. Therefore, we must choose our company wisely and correct bad behaviour early, before it spreads. Good company helps us grow, while bad company drags us down.

answers.label: Q.6
answers.solution:
The Winning Pass

It was the final match of the summer football camp. The Dark team and the White team were level at one goal each, and only two minutes were left. Parents cheered loudly from the edge of the field.

Riya was the only girl in the White team. On the first day of the camp, some boys had laughed at her. 'Football is not for girls,' Kabir had said. Riya said nothing. She simply came early every morning and practised her dribbling until the sun was high.

Now the ball rolled towards Arjun, the Dark team's fastest player. Before he could shoot, Sam from the White team tackled him and pushed the ball forward. Riya sprinted after it, her hair flying in the wind. Two defenders closed in on her. Instead of shooting, she passed the ball to Kabir, who stood unmarked, and he kicked it straight into the net!

The whistle blew. The White team had won. Kabir ran to Riya and shook her hand. 'I was wrong about you,' he said with a smile.

That day, everyone learnt that hard work and teamwork matter more than anything else.

answers.label: Q.7
answers.solution:
My Favourite Video Game: Minecraft

Of all the video games I have played, my favourite is Minecraft, a game in which the whole world is made of blocks and the only limit is my imagination. When I start a new world, I find myself standing in a vast landscape of green meadows, dark forests, snowy mountains and shimmering blue oceans, all built from tiny square blocks. The sun rises slowly over the hills, sheep and cows wander lazily across the grass, and soft piano music in the background makes everything feel calm and peaceful. My first task is always to collect wood from a tree, which I turn into planks, a crafting table and simple tools. With a wooden pickaxe in hand, I dig into the grey stone and discover glittering lumps of coal and iron and, if I am very lucky, sparkling blue diamonds hidden deep underground. As the sky turns orange and then black, the mood of the game changes completely: zombies groan in the darkness, skeletons rattle their bones, and the silent green Creeper sneaks up with a frightening hiss. This is when my small shelter, lit by flickering torches, becomes the safest place in the world. What I love most about Minecraft is that it lets me create anything I can dream of. I have built a tall castle with towers and a drawbridge, a farm with neat rows of wheat and carrots, and even a railway that winds through the mountains. Every creation teaches me something new: planning a building needs measurement and patience, collecting resources needs careful management, and the redstone circuits work like real electric wiring, which has made me curious about science. I also enjoy playing with my cousin, because we divide the work, one of us mining while the other builds, and in this way we learn to cooperate and solve problems together. Unlike many games that are only about fighting and winning, Minecraft rewards creativity, planning and teamwork. Of course, I make sure that I play only after finishing my homework and never for more than an hour a day. For me, Minecraft is not just a game; it is a colourful world of adventure where I can be an explorer, an architect and an inventor all at once.

answers.label: Q.8
answers.finalAnswer: conjunction; adjective; pronoun; adjective
answers.solution:
(a) Though: conjunction. It joins the two clauses 'he was angry' and 'he remained calm'.
(b) miserly: adjective. It describes the noun 'person'.
(c) Each: pronoun (distributive pronoun). It stands alone in place of a noun ('each of you').
(d) Each: adjective (distributive adjective). It comes before and qualifies the noun 'boy'.

answers.label: Q.9
answers.finalAnswer: I took breakfast two seconds ago; The Prime Minister leaves for London tomorrow; He came to my house after I had had my lunch; She came to my house while I was reading a novel
answers.solution:
(a) I took breakfast two seconds ago.
Rule: the present perfect is not used with a word of past time such as 'ago'; use the simple past.

(b) The Prime Minister leaves for London tomorrow.
Rule: the simple present is used for a fixed, planned future programme. (The sentence as printed, with 'will leave', is also grammatically acceptable, so this item has no clear error.)

(c) He came to my house after I had had my lunch.
Rule: of two past actions, the one that happened first takes the past perfect.

(d) She came to my house while I was reading a novel.
Rule: an action in progress when another action happened takes the past continuous.

answers.label: Q.10
answers.finalAnswer: No other footballer in the world is as good as Lionel Messi; We do not know the girl's address; He was poor, but he continued to have big dreams; Who does not admire Mahender Singh Dhoni?; The soldier who was fearless was able to kill five terrorists single-handedly; No sooner did we reach the stadium than the coach shouted at us; The meal was cooked by the chef; Raju said, "I completed the assignment yesterday."; Why was the car not liked by your sister?; Meena proposed to Tina that they should go to the theatre the next day
answers.solution:
(a) No other footballer in the world is as good as Lionel Messi.
(Superlative changed to a negative comparison.)

(b) We do not know the girl's address.
(The noun clause 'where the girl lives' becomes the noun phrase 'the girl's address'.)

(c) He was poor, but he continued to have big dreams.
(Two main clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction 'but'.)

(d) Who does not admire Mahender Singh Dhoni?
(A statement turned into a question with the same meaning.)

(e) The soldier who was fearless was able to kill five terrorists single-handedly.
(The adjective 'fearless' becomes the relative clause 'who was fearless'.)

(f) No sooner did we reach the stadium than the coach shouted at us.
('As soon as' becomes 'No sooner ... than'.)

(g) The meal was cooked by the chef.

(h) Raju said, "I completed the assignment yesterday."
(Past perfect becomes simple past; 'the previous day' becomes 'yesterday'; 'he' becomes 'I'.)

(i) Why was the car not liked by your sister?

(j) Meena proposed to Tina that they should go to the theatre the next day.
('Let's' becomes 'proposed/suggested that they should'; 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.)

answers.label: Q.11
answers.finalAnswer: to have butterflies in one's stomach; in the blink of an eye; to fight shy of; to play to the gallery; in the air
answers.solution:
(a) To be excited or nervous: to have butterflies in one's stomach.
Example: I had butterflies in my stomach before the interview.

(b) Quickly or very fast: in the blink of an eye (also: in a jiffy, like a shot).
Example: The thief disappeared in the blink of an eye.

(c) To avoid or shy away from danger: to fight shy of.
Example: A brave soldier never fights shy of danger.

(d) To do something to get the attention of others: to play to the gallery.
Example: The leader's speech was only playing to the gallery.

(e) Of a feeling being felt by everyone: in the air.
Example: On the last day of school, excitement was in the air.

answers.label: Q.12
answers.finalAnswer: graphology; bibliophobia; apiary; caddie; irony
answers.solution:
(a) Study of handwriting: graphology
(b) Fear of books: bibliophobia
(c) A place for keeping bees: apiary
(d) A person who helps a golfer: caddie (also spelt caddy)
(e) A figure of speech in which one says the opposite of what is meant: irony

answers.label: Q.13
answers.finalAnswer: demonstrative adjective; possessive adjective; past participle (verb); personal pronoun (objective case); interrogative pronoun
answers.solution:
(a) This: demonstrative adjective (determiner). It points out the noun 'car'.
(b) my: possessive adjective (possessive determiner). It shows whose car it is.
(c) left: past participle of the verb 'leave', used in the passive 'was left'.
(d) them: personal pronoun in the objective case, the object of the preposition 'by'.
(e) What: interrogative pronoun. It asks a question and stands for the thing asked about.

answers.label: Q.14
answers.finalAnswer: Match: a game / a matchstick; Watch: a timepiece / to look at; Ring: an ornament for the finger / to sound a bell; Point: a sharp tip / the main idea; Bear: a wild animal / to tolerate
answers.solution:
(a) Match
1. A game or contest: India won the cricket match.
2. A small stick used to light a fire: She lit the lamp with a match.

(b) Watch
1. A small clock worn on the wrist: My father gifted me a watch.
2. To look at carefully: We watch the news every evening.

(c) Ring
1. A round ornament worn on the finger: She wears a gold ring.
2. To make a bell sound: Ring the bell when the period ends.

(d) Point
1. The sharp end of something: The point of my pencil broke.
2. The main idea: He made a strong point in the debate.

(e) Bear
1. A large wild animal: We saw a black bear at the zoo.
2. To tolerate: I cannot bear this noise.
